explanations: terra: Twelve springs gush from the struck stone, every group knows its drinking place, and all are told to eat and drink God's provision without corruption.
terra: Israel voices dissatisfaction with one food and asks Moses for earthly varieties, showing appetite directing speech despite existing provision.

luna: This covenant command joins care for parents, kin, orphans, and the poor to وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا, speaking well to people, as the section joins bodily speech with care for the vulnerable. | terra: The covenant joins care for kin, orphans, and the needy with speaking good to people, directing resources and utterance toward others together.
terra: Believers are likewise commanded to eat good provision and thank God, a repeated formulation of responsible reception.

luna: The section joins release of a neck to feeding the vulnerable; this ayah places care for kin, orphans, and the poor alongside giving فِي الرِّقَابِ, faith, patience, and keeping one's word. | terra: Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans, needy people, travelers, beggars, and “the necks,” gathering feeding's social field and liberation.
terra: Those unable to fast have a compensating duty of feeding a needy person, making another mouth's food the concrete substitute for a bodily act of restraint.
terra: A person's speech about worldly life can impress while his heart is fiercely hostile, distinguishing attractive mouth-output from inward stance.
terra: The response to a question about spending directs good wealth to parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, specifying the outward destination of possession.

luna: The section's ط ع م lexicon includes tasting, and its secondary lip image includes water crowded by mouths; here soldiers drink from a river under a one-handful limit, putting the same tasting root on water and showing measured access. The verse does not say the river is depleted. | terra: The river test distinguishes drinking from merely taking a handful, and uses يَطْعَمْهُ for tasting it, directly illustrating طعم as taste applied to water.
terra: Those who spend without following their gift with reminders or injury preserve reward, clarifying the giving-and-speech measure stated in 2:263.

luna: The section's outward mouth can speak well while its inward work gives food; this ayah says a good word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury. | terra: A recognized good word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, judging what leaves the mouth alongside what the hand gives.
terra: Believers are told not to nullify charity with reminders and injury, showing harmful output undoing the value of outward provision.
terra: Hidden needy people refrain from importunate asking and may be mistaken for self-sufficient, requiring perception rather than waiting for a hungry mouth to insist.

luna: The section's womb and bodily-formation scene meets Allah's forming people in wombs as He wills. | terra: God forms humans in wombs however He wills, presenting prenatal bodily shaping as deliberate divine work.

luna: The section makes the tongue the organ of speech; this ayah depicts people twisting their tongues while presenting words as scripture, a concrete misuse of the organ. | terra: A group twist their tongues with the Book so listeners mistake human distortion for revelation, a concrete wrong turning of the speaking organ.
terra: People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, setting the relinquishment of prized possession against boast over wealth.
terra: Hatred has appeared from enemies' mouths while their breasts conceal more, showing speech emerging from and partially exposing the body's interior.
terra: Hypocrites say with their mouths what is not in their hearts, separating the speaking instrument's output from inward truth.
terra: What misers withhold will be collared around their necks at resurrection, joining hoarded wealth to the very body part liberation should free.
luna: The section calls for food to go toward an orphan's mouth; this ayah forbids consuming orphan property together with one's own, the opposite direction of taking and giving.
terra: Dependants are to be fed and clothed from property and spoken to with a recognized good word, again pairing provision with responsible speech.

luna: The section joins the mouth's two works: giving food and speaking well. This ayah commands provision from an inheritance for present kin, orphans, and needy people together with قولًا معروفًا, a recognized good word. | terra: At distribution, relatives, orphans, and the poor must be provided from the estate and addressed with a recognized good قول, commanding the mouth's material and verbal work together.

luna: The section's feeding action is inverted: unjustly consuming an orphan's wealth becomes fire in the consumer's own belly. | terra: Those who wrongfully consume orphans' property are only eating fire into their bellies, reversing food's nourishing entry and the duty toward the orphan.
terra: Care for relatives, orphans, needy people, neighbors, travelers, and dependants is set against the arrogant boaster whom God does not love.
terra: The miserly both withhold and command others to withhold while concealing God's bounty, misdirecting possession and outward speech together.
luna: The section's dictionary sense of face-to-face speech is a two-way exchange; this ayah tells the person who receives a greeting to answer with a better one or return it.

luna: The section's action فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ releases a person; this ayah uses the same neck-for-person expression in requiring the freeing of a believing neck as expiation. | terra: The accidental killer must free a believing neck, another direct Qur'anic instance of the emancipatory action named by فك رقبة.
terra: Private speech is mostly without good unless it commands charity, recognized good, or reconciliation, directing talk toward material and social benefit.
terra: Some say “we believe” with their mouths although their hearts have not believed, another explicit misuse of mouth-to-mouth profession.
terra: The Messiah and his mother both ate food; ordinary bodily intake proves their creaturely dependence despite exalted claims about them.

luna: The section joins neck-release to feeding; this oath expiation offers freeing a neck or feeding ten needy people, directly pairing the two acts. | terra: Expiation for spoken oaths includes feeding ten needy people or freeing a neck, uniting the section's mouth, food, and فك رقبة in one ayah.

luna: The section develops asking and giving around food; here the disciples make a spoken request for a table sent down from heaven. | terra: The disciples ask whether a table can be sent from heaven, staging spoken request for a shared source of food.

luna: The section brings outward speech together with inward eating; the disciples explain that they want to eat from the heavenly table, have their hearts reassured, and know that Jesus has told them the truth. | terra: They say they want to eat from the table so their hearts are reassured, making the mouth's inward act the desired confirmation.

luna: This ayah is Jesus' spoken request to God for the table and its provision, completing the section's relation between a request and food given. | terra: Jesus asks God to send the table as a feast, sign, and provision, joining prayerful speech to divinely given food.

luna: The section's dictionary form makes feeding a relation between giver and recipient; this ayah names Allah as the One who feeds and is not fed. | terra: God is described as the One who feeds and is not fed, establishing the ultimate asymmetry behind the section's one person asking and another giving food.
terra: God can take hearing and sight and seal hearts, making explicit that bodily faculties are contingent gifts rather than owned powers.
terra: Guidance is pictured as God expanding a chest for surrender, while misguidance makes it tight and constricted, turning the chest in two opposed directions.
terra: People may eat harvest fruit but must give its due and avoid waste, placing personal consumption beside another's material claim.
terra: “When you speak, be just,” even concerning a relative, subjects the organ's outward act to the same moral measure as property and covenant.
terra: Humans may eat and drink but must not be excessive, placing a moral measure on the mouth's inward work.
terra: The repeated twelve-spring scene assigns each tribe its watering place and commands eating from good provision, ordering many mouths around supplied water.

luna: The section asks how given organs are used; this ayah pictures people with hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear, a specific failure of those faculties. | terra: People have hearts, eyes, and ears but do not use them for understanding, seeing, or hearing, the clearest reversal of properly directed bodily tools.
terra: Hostile people please believers with their mouths while their hearts refuse, a vivid mouth-to-mouth address divided from inward stance.
terra: False theological claims are called an utterance of their mouths, marking the embodied output as imitation rather than grounded truth.
terra: Opponents seek to extinguish God's light with their mouths, assigning destructive intention to the same bodily outlet made for speech.

luna: The section's فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ is bodily release; this alms list again names في الرقاب among the people supported by charity, alongside the poor and needy. | terra: Obligatory charity is assigned both to the poor and needy and to “the necks,” placing material relief and emancipation in the same distribution.
terra: Those unable to find transport leave with eyes overflowing in grief because they lack something to spend, turning sight and absent wealth toward sincere need.
terra: The hearers are asked who provides from heaven and earth and who controls hearing and sight, joining bodily faculties to the source of provision.
terra: No recitation, deed, or act escapes God's witnessing when people engage in it, a broader assurance that spoken activity is seen.
terra: People fold their chests to hide, yet God knows what they conceal and reveal, joining a body part to the failure of imagined invisibility.

luna: The section says one may ask another to speak and develops food and speech as two mouth-functions; here a prisoner asks Yusuf to interpret dreams that feature pressed drink and bread eaten by birds.
luna: The section's dictionary sense joins requesting food with speech; Yusuf says he will tell the prisoners the interpretation before their food arrives, placing speech and a meal in one scene.
terra: Joseph's brothers say hardship has touched them and ask for full measure and charity, a concrete hungry mouth addressing one able to provide.
luna: The section's neck can be freed; this ayah pictures collars around necks in its account of those who reject resurrection.
terra: Calling false gods is compared to one stretching hands toward water so it will reach his mouth, yet it never does, directly staging sought water and an unfilled mouth.

luna: The section calls لسان the speech organ; this ayah describes each messenger speaking in his people's tongue so the message is clear to them. | terra: Each messenger is sent in the tongue or language of his people so he can make the message clear, extending the physical organ into intelligible communal speech.
terra: Rejecting peoples put their hands to their mouths and verbally deny their messengers, combining bodily gesture and resistant speech.
terra: The arrogant are given putrid water to drink, turning the sought drink of the mouth into punishment.
terra: The drinker tries to gulp it but can scarcely swallow, a precise reversal of the opened throat through which provision should enter.
terra: God sends fertilizing winds and water from heaven for people to drink while they are not its storekeepers, sharply distinguishing giver from recipient.
terra: God knows the Prophet's chest is constricted by what hostile people say, tracing painful outward speech into a bodily interior.
terra: God creates the human from a drop, yet the human becomes a manifest disputant, the same turn from dependent body to self-asserting speech.
terra: Pure milk comes for drinkers from within cattle bellies between waste and blood, making an inward body region the workshop of mouth-ready provision.

luna: The section's body begins in the mother's womb; this ayah says people emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then names hearing, sight, and hearts as given faculties. | terra: God brings humans from their mothers' bellies knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; the body and its faculties are expressly bestowed tools calling for gratitude.
luna: The section's bodily لسان extends to spoken language here, where the charge of a foreign informant is answered by the clear Arabic tongue of the message.
terra: The hearers must eat lawful good provision and thank God for His favor, turning received food toward gratitude.

luna: The section asks what an outward-speaking mouth is used for; this ayah condemns tongues that falsely declare what is lawful and forbidden. | terra: The addressees must not let their tongues falsely label things lawful and unlawful, because that bodily utterance fabricates a lie against God.
terra: Every person's record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an open book, remarkably joining the section's neck with its dictionary image of unsealing a book.
terra: The person is commanded to read his own book and suffice as his own reckoner, bringing the opened record through the mouth into self-accounting.
terra: The relative, needy person, and traveler are to receive their due, directing owned provision outward rather than into boast or waste.
terra: If one must turn from those claimants while awaiting provision, one must still speak an easy word to them, preserving the mouth's good outward work when it cannot give.
terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor wholly outspread, using two named body parts to measure miserliness and waste around 17:26–28.

luna: The section asks how the body's tools are used; this ayah says hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned about their use. | terra: Hearing, sight, and heart are each subject to questioning, explicitly stating the accountability of furnished faculties.
terra: The arrogant walker can neither split the earth nor equal mountains in height, exposing the limits of the upright body that displays pride.
terra: People ask aloud whether they will be raised after becoming bones and fragments, joining decayed bodily parts with disputing speech.
terra: The answer identifies the One who originated them the first time, while their own mouths ask who will restore them.
terra: God commands His servants to say what is best because Satan can sow division between them, showing the interpersonal consequence of the mouth's direction.

luna: The section derives the right-side designation from the hand; this ayah calls people by their record, with the successful receiving it in the right hand. | terra: Those given their record in their right hands read it, joining right hand, opened book, and the mouth's act of reading.
terra: A grave claim is described as a word coming out of their mouths, foregrounding the outward bodily passage and moral weight of speech.
terra: The Prophet is told to keep with humble worshippers and not let his eyes pass beyond them seeking worldly adornment, directing sight away from wealth-status.
terra: Hell's drink is like molten liquid that scalds faces, a specific contrary image in which bringing drink to the mouth destroys the visible body.
terra: The garden owner says during direct conversation that he has more wealth and a stronger following, closely paralleling boast issued from a wealthy mouth.
terra: Entering his garden, he says he does not think it will ever perish, making his spoken confidence in possession explicit.
terra: His companion answers by recalling that God created him from dust and a drop and then proportioned him as a man, confronting wealth-boast with bodily making.
terra: The companion supplies the right garden utterance—acknowledging God's will and that power belongs to God—against the owner's boast.
terra: Moses and his companion ask a town's people for food and are denied hospitality, directly enacting the dictionary relation in which one asks to be fed and another may give.
terra: Abraham and his family are granted mercy and an exalted “tongue of truth,” repeating the nonphysical outcome produced by truthful remembrance and speech.
terra: The human is asked to remember that God created him before he was anything, a direct correction of made humanity's self-sufficiency.

luna: Moses asks for his chest to be opened, meeting the section's lexicographic chest reading for بلد and its bodily frame for speech. | terra: Moses asks for his chest to be expanded before asking for the tongue's knot to be untied; the bodily prayer coheres with the section's chest-and-mouth inventory.

luna: The section presents لسان as the organ that speaks; Moses asks for the knot in his tongue to be loosened. | terra: Moses asks God to untie a knot from his tongue, joining the physical speaking organ with the section's image of opening what is bound.

luna: The section joins tongue and utterance as organ and work; Moses asks that others understand his قول, his speech. | terra: The requested result is that people understand Moses' قول, placing tongue and utterance together exactly as the section joins lisān and yaqūlu.
terra: The Prophet must not extend his eyes toward others' worldly splendor; God's provision is better and more lasting, joining sight to the appraisal of provision.

luna: The section cites the dictionary form مُخَلَّقَةٌ for a fully formed morsel; this creation sequence explicitly contrasts a formed and unformed morsel. | terra: The womb contains a lump مُّخَلَّقَةٍ وَغَيْرِ مُخَلَّقَةٍ, the very Qur'anic form behind the section's dictionary example of a fully formed piece of flesh.
terra: Pilgrims are told to eat sacrificial animals and feed the distressed poor, giving the mouth both reception and outward provision in one command.
terra: Avoidance of false قول is commanded beside avoidance of idols, giving speech a concrete boundary rather than treating it as neutral output.

luna: This ayah pairs eating with feeding the contented and the needy from the sacrifice; it gives the section's inward mouth-work a concrete sharing scene. | terra: The worshippers may eat from the sacrificial camels and feed both the contented and the petitioner, again dividing food between one's own mouth and others.
terra: The ayah says bodily eyes do not become blind; rather, hearts within chests do, distinguishing possession of an organ from its right perceptive use.
terra: Human creation begins from an extract of clay, adding the elemental material behind the later part-by-part body.
terra: God places the reproductive drop in a secure lodging, supplying the womb-stage immediately before the lump, bones, and flesh of 23:14.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss of مُضْغَةٌ مُخَلَّقَةٌ is completed formation; here the morsel is followed by bones clothed with flesh and another creation. | terra: The drop becomes clot, lump, bones clothed with flesh, then “another creation,” staging the craftsman-like, part-by-part making of the body.
terra: God sends water in due measure, lodges it in the earth, and declares His ability to remove it, exposing every drinking mouth's dependence on measured provision.
terra: Livestock bellies yield drink, while the animals also supply many benefits and food, joining bodily interior, drinking, and eating as provision.
terra: Messengers are commanded to eat good things and do right, coupling bodily intake with the action expected from its recipients.

luna: This ayah says Allah originated people and made hearing, sight, and hearts, the faculties that make the section's question about bodily tools concrete. | terra: God produces humans and gives them hearing, eyes, and hearts, yet they give little thanks, directly treating organs as bestowed and answerable faculties.

luna: The section treats the tongue as a speech organ; this ayah depicts people passing words from tongue to tongue without knowledge and thinking the matter slight. | terra: People pass a rumor with their tongues and say with their mouths what they do not know, while deeming it slight though it is grave with God.

luna: The section says the given organs are tools with consequences; here tongues, hands, and feet testify against their owners. | terra: Tongues, hands, and feet testify against their owners, so the speaking organ becomes accountable rather than remaining its owner's obedient instrument.
terra: Believing men are commanded to lower their gaze, giving the endowed eyes a concrete disciplined direction.
luna: The section names freeing a neck as a bodily act; this ayah gives enslaved people a written path to emancipation and directs others to help them from God's provision.
terra: When the ignorant address the servants of the Merciful, they answer with peace, giving mouth-to-mouth exchange a restrained direction.

luna: Moses describes his chest tightening and his tongue not setting free; the bodily impediment makes the section's chest, tongue, and speech links concrete. | terra: Moses says his chest tightens and his tongue does not move freely, bringing chest, tongue, and obstructed outward speech into one body.

luna: The section links creation to guidance as a sequence; Abraham confesses that the One who created him is the One who guides him. | terra: Abraham confesses that the One who created him is the One who guides him, matching the section's creation-to-guidance sequence.

luna: The section's inward work of the mouth is feeding; Abraham says that his Lord feeds him and gives him drink. | terra: Abraham next says God feeds and gives him drink, completing the section's sequence from creation and guidance to the mouth's reception of provision.
terra: Abraham asks for “a tongue of truth” among later people, extending lisān from the bodily speaking organ to enduring truthful repute.
luna: The section treats the tongue as the organ of speech; this ayah describes the revelation as being on a clear Arabic tongue.

luna: The section's dictionary water image is a source crowded by people; this ayah places a crowd watering flocks at the water of Midian while two women wait apart. It does not say people drink or that the water is exhausted, so the parallel is limited to a shared gathering at a water source. | terra: Moses reaches a water source crowded by people watering while two women hold back, closely realizing the section's secondary scene of heavily sought water.
terra: Moses waters for the women and then declares his own need for whatever good God sends, turning competition at water into provision for another and a request for provision.
terra: Moses calls Aaron more fluent than himself in tongue and asks that he support his message, treating the tongue as the working tool of address.
terra: Qārūn's treasure keys burden a company of strong men, establishing the mass of wealth and bodily strength answered by his boast in 28:78.
terra: Qārūn is told to use what God gave for the lasting abode, do good as God did good to him, and not seek corruption, a direct rule for a bestowed resource's direction.
terra: Qārūn replies that his wealth came by his own knowledge, but is reminded that God destroyed generations stronger than he, pairing mouth-boast with the limit of power.
terra: “Everything is perishing except His face” gives هالك its absolute sense and places the boast of expended wealth within what cannot remain.
terra: God's creation of humans from dust precedes their spreading as living people, a concise transition from base material to completed bodies.
terra: Differences in human languages and colors are signs of God, placing tongues or languages within the deliberately varied made body.
luna: The section names both birth from the womb and كَبَدٍ as hardship; this ayah makes bodily bearing a form of hardship for the mother.
terra: Turning one's cheek from people and walking arrogantly are forbidden because God does not love the proud boaster, placing pride visibly in the body.
terra: Measured walking and a lowered voice are commanded together, directing bodily posture and mouth-produced sound toward restraint.

luna: The section asks what the bestowed body parts are for; this ayah describes the human being fashioned and given hearing, sight, and hearts, then asks for gratitude. | terra: God proportions the human, breathes into him, and makes hearing, sight, and hearts; formed body and usable faculties are one gift.
terra: Human social fictions are called “your saying with your mouths,” while God says truth and guides the way, opposing mouth-made claim to true قول and guidance.
terra: Cowards assail believers with sharp tongues while greedy for benefit, joining injurious speech to acquisitive appetite in one bodily portrait.
terra: Believers are commanded to speak a straight, sound قول, giving the section's tongue an explicitly right-directed outward task.
terra: The affluent say, “We are greater in wealth and children, and we will not be punished,” another explicit wealth-boast that presumes immunity.
terra: Wealth and children do not bring one near to God; faith and right action do, correcting the immunity-boast spoken in 34:35.
terra: Creation from dust and a drop proceeds to pairs and wombs whose pregnancies God knows, joining bodily material, formation, and divine knowledge.

luna: The section presents freeing a neck; this ayah depicts necks encircled by shackles and chins forced upward, the bodily opposite of release. | terra: Shackles rise to the disbelievers' necks and force their heads upward, turning the upright neck from a free bodily posture into constraint.

luna: The section's ط ع م form puts asking and feeding in relation; here those with provision reject the request to spend and ask, أَنُطْعِمُ, whether they should feed someone Allah could feed. | terra: When told to spend from God's provision, disbelievers answer aloud, “Should we feed” someone God could feed; their mouth uses speech to refuse another mouth food.

luna: The section's boast comes from a speaking mouth and a body equipped with limbs; this ayah seals mouths and lets hands and feet speak, reversing which bodily parts give testimony. | terra: God seals their mouths while hands speak and feet testify; the boasting mouth is stopped and another bodily witness takes over.
terra: Though created from a drop, the human becomes an open disputant, juxtaposing made body and boastful mouth.
terra: He voices a parable about decayed bones and forgets his own creation, making wrong speech arise from forgetfulness of bodily making.
terra: The commanded answer says the One who originated the bones will revive them, restoring the Maker's power over every part.

luna: The section brings the formed body back to its prenatal beginning; this ayah describes creation within mothers' wombs, form after form in three darknesses. | terra: Humans are created in their mothers' wombs, creation after creation in three darknesses, extending the image of a body made stage by stage.
terra: Those who listen to speech and follow its best are called guided, placing reception and selection of قول within the path of right use.
terra: A chest expanded for surrender stands in God's light, giving the secondary chest image a spiritual orientation toward guidance.
terra: At the approaching day hearts rise to throats as people choke back anguish, using the throat to show bodily helplessness at accountability.
terra: God knows the treachery of eyes and what chests conceal, joining two enumerated bodily regions to the answer to “did no one see him?”
terra: God forms humans and makes their forms beautiful, then provides good things, joining bodily craftsmanship to what enters and sustains the made body.

luna: The section follows bodily making through birth and formed limbs; this ayah traces human life from dust and a drop through an infant, maturity, and old age. | terra: One ayah surveys creation from dust, drop, clot, childhood, maturity, and old age, supporting the section's made body through its successive completed states.
terra: Collars are placed around necks and the condemned are dragged in chains, a bodily reversal of releasing a neck.
terra: ʿĀd boast aloud, “Who is stronger than us?” and are answered that their Creator is stronger, directly reversing imagined bodily power.

luna: The section's body is made of distinct organs; at judgment, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners. | terra: At judgment hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, turning the body's granted parts into witnesses of how they were used.

luna: The section lists body parts as made organs; here the skin itself answers that Allah enabled it to speak, extending testimony beyond the human mouth. | terra: The condemned address their own skins and ask why they testified; the body's parts answer within the scene begun in 41:20.

luna: The section's man assumes no one sees him; this ayah says people did not hide from their own hearing, eyes, and skins, but thought Allah did not know much of what they did. | terra: They did not expect hearing, eyes, and skins to testify and thought God did not know much of what they did, directly reversing the section's man who thinks no one sees him.
terra: Pharaoh publicly proclaims his kingdom and flowing rivers and asks his people whether they see, combining boastful mouth, possession, and manipulated sight.
terra: Those who suppose God does not hear their secrets and private talk are told that His messengers record it, answering the boast spoken under imagined invisibility.
terra: The tree of Zaqqūm is called the food of the sinner, making food itself carry judgment.
luna: The section contrasts food that should nourish with consumption that turns to punishment; this ayah names food for the sinner, a direct contrary meal.

luna: The section says unjust consumption can become fire in the belly; after 44:44 names food for the sinner, this ayah's own contribution is that it boils in the bellies, reversing food's nourishing role. | terra: That food is like molten substance boiling in bellies, turning the body's interior from recipient of nourishment into a site of torment.
terra: The person who makes desire his god has hearing and heart sealed and a covering over sight, a judgmental reversal of the organs first bestowed.

luna: The section's body is equipped with hearing, sight, and hearts; this ayah says those faculties did not avail a people when they rejected the signs. | terra: The hearing, sight, and hearts granted to a powerful people availed them nothing when they rejected God's signs, showing endowed tools failing through their use.
terra: Combat begins with striking necks and binding captives before release or ransom, the violent and captive boundary against which “freeing a neck” signifies mercy.
terra: Paradise's unspoiled drink is opposed to boiling water that cuts intestines, setting a bodily boundary between provision and punitive ingestion.
terra: People invited to spend in God's path may become miserly, and their miserliness turns back upon themselves.
terra: The desert Arabs say with their tongues what is not in their hearts, exposing the tongue as a tool capable of divided direction.
terra: Backbiting is pictured as eating the flesh of one's dead brother, fusing the mouth's outward injury and inward eating into one repellent reversal.
terra: God created the human, knows the self's whisper, and is nearer than the jugular vein, making bodily intimacy the answer to imagined concealment.

luna: The section sets a boastful utterance beside the belief that no one sees the speaker; this ayah says no قول is uttered without a watcher ready beside the speaker. | terra: No قول is uttered without a watcher ready to record it, directly answering the speaker who thinks no one sees his boast.
terra: The righteous acknowledge in their wealth a right for the asker and the deprived, a direct counterimage to wealth spoken of as one's private feat.
terra: The hearers are directed to signs “in yourselves,” inviting the made body itself to answer the section's catalogue of organs.
terra: Abraham quietly brings a fat calf to his guests, staging food offered from one person toward other mouths.
terra: He places the food near them and asks whether they will eat, joining offered provision and face-to-face speech.
terra: God says He seeks neither provision nor feeding from creatures, setting the dependent human mouth against the self-sufficient giver.
terra: God is the provider and possessor of firm power, grounding the asymmetry in 51:57 and the section's supplied bodily tools.
terra: The Prophet's sight neither swerved nor transgressed at the vision, presenting exact and bounded use of the eye.
luna: The section names the body before and after birth; this ayah recalls people as embryos in their mothers' wombs.

luna: This ayah explicitly says Allah created the human, matching the section's body as a made, assembled thing; its next ayah specifies an outward human faculty. | terra: “Created the human” begins a two-ayah sequence in which bodily creation is immediately followed by the gift of expression.

luna: The section calls لسان the speech organ; this ayah names البيان, articulate expression, as something taught to the human. | terra: God “taught him البيان,” making articulate speech a created human capacity just as the section treats the tongue and lips as furnished instruments.
terra: Everyone upon the earth passes away, a nonfinancial use of the destruction root that strips bodily possession of permanence.
terra: The majestic face of the Lord remains after 55:26's universal passing, fixing the boundary between made body and enduring Maker.

luna: The section explains الميمنة as the side named from the right hand; this ayah repeats the designation أصحاب الميمنة for the people of the right. | terra: أَصْحَابُ ٱلْمَيْمَنَةِ exactly repeats the section's title for the people of the right side and asks what their state will be.

luna: This paired ayah names أصحاب المشأمة opposite the right-side party, making the bodily right/left boundary in the section's term visible. | terra: The people of the left are named immediately opposite the people of the right, defining meymena's moral and spatial boundary.

luna: This later passage again calls a saved group أصحاب اليمين, repeating the section's movement from right-hand wording to a group designation. | terra: أَصْحَابُ ٱلْيَمِينِ restates the same company through the right hand or right side, clarifying meymena's bodily orientation.
terra: The astray are told they will eat from the tree of Zaqqūm, turning the mouth's inward work into punishment.
terra: They fill their bellies from Zaqqūm, making bodily fullness itself the reverse of merciful nourishment.
terra: They then drink boiling water over the punitive food, completing a meal in which both inward acts of the mouth harm the body.
terra: The addressee is made to consider the reproductive fluid he emits, beginning a challenge about who actually fashions the body.
terra: “Do you create it, or are We the creators?” directly overturns the human's illusion of autonomous bodily power.
terra: God says He apportioned death among humans and cannot be outstripped, setting the Maker's power against bodily confidence.
terra: God can replace humans with their likes and produce them in forms they do not know, extending bodily workmanship beyond the present form.

luna: The section's dictionary image has mouths seeking water; this ayah asks about the water people drink and who sends it from the clouds. It gives a concrete drinking-and-provision parallel, but does not mention crowding or depletion. | terra: “Have you considered the water you drink?” makes the mouth's received water an occasion to recognize the giver.
terra: The question asks whether humans sent drinking water down from the clouds or God did, identifying the provider between 56:68's drink and 56:70's threatened bitterness.
terra: God could make that water bitter, revealing the drink's dependence and the boundary on the drinker's access.
terra: The departing life reaches the throat while human onlookers stand helpless, making the mouth's bodily passage a scene of lost control.
terra: God is nearer to the dying person than the watchers, though they cannot see, reversing the supposition that unseen presence means no one witnesses.
terra: The hearers are challenged to return the departing life if they are truthful, exposing the hard limit on human power over the body.
terra: The dying person may be among the people of the right, carrying the right-side classification into the body's final passage.
terra: A greeting of peace is addressed to that person “from the people of the right,” adding beneficent speech to the right-side scene.

luna: The section treats outward speech as a bodily act with consequences; this ayah itself calls the marital utterance blameworthy and false, and 58:3 supplies the following neck-freeing expiation. | terra: A husband's bodily comparison of his wife to his mother's back is condemned as an objectionable falsehood, the harmful mouth-act corrected by freeing and feeding in 58:3–4.

luna: The section's outward speech and release of the neck meet in a legal consequence of a spoken marital formula: before the couple touches, the speaker must free a neck. | terra: A wrongful bodily declaration about one's wife is answered by freeing a neck before contact, turning harmful speech into a duty of release.

luna: This continuation pairs the section's two mouth directions with neck-release: if the person cannot free a neck or fast, the expiation is feeding sixty poor people. | terra: Whoever cannot free the neck must eventually feed sixty needy people, continuing the same correction from mouth-made wrong to another mouth's nourishment.
terra: God knows every secret consultation and is present by knowledge wherever its speakers are, setting a boundary on supposedly private speech.
terra: Charity is required before private consultation with the Messenger, placing a material act before the privilege of spoken exchange.
terra: The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, a specific reversal of letting one's appetite or possession close against another.
terra: Believers are asked why they say what they do not do, directly making utterance answerable to action.
terra: God greatly hates saying what one does not do, completing 61:2's judgment of irresponsible output from the mouth.
terra: The repeated attempt to extinguish God's light with mouths gives a second direct image of speech used against revelation.
terra: God created humans and made their forms beautiful, then names return to Him, linking finished bodily form with accountability.
terra: Whether speech is concealed or voiced, God knows what lies in breasts, directly relating mouth, hidden chest, and divine knowledge.
terra: “Would the One who created not know?” grounds the knowledge of 67:13 in the Maker's intimate knowledge of the made body.

luna: The section treats eyes and speech organs as given tools; this ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts as Allah's gifts and asks why people give so little thanks. | terra: The addressee is reminded that God produced them and made hearing, eyes, and hearts, yet they give little thanks, directly posing the section's question about use of organs.
terra: The addressee must consider who could bring flowing water if their water sank away, exposing the hidden dependence behind every mouthful.
terra: The Prophet is told not to obey a habitual swearer, beginning a portrait of a mouth repeatedly turned to corrupt output.
terra: The same figure is a slanderer who circulates malicious speech, specifying the tongue's interpersonal harm.
terra: He actively hinders good, transgresses, and sins, connecting the wrong-speaking figure to blocked benefit for others.
terra: His wealth and children explain his presumption, joining the corrupt mouth of 68:10–11 to confidence in possessions.
terra: The garden owners whisper that no needy person may enter upon them that day, using speech to shut their crop away from another mouth.
terra: When the garden is ruined they say, “Rather, we are deprived,” making the would-be deprivers experience deprivation.
terra: The most balanced among them recalls that he had urged them to glorify God, preserving a right spoken intervention inside the withholding scene.

luna: The section explains the right-side group through the word for the right hand; this judgment scene gives one person his record in his right hand, where the bodily word carries an outcome. | terra: The person given his book in his right hand speaks and invites others to read it, combining right hand, mouth, and accountable record.
terra: “Eat and drink pleasantly” is the reward announced in the right-hand recipient's scene, aligning the mouth's reception with prior deeds.

luna: The section links الميمنة to the right hand; this paired judgment scene gives another person his record in the left hand, marking the opposite outcome. | terra: The person given his book in his left hand speaks regretfully, reversing the right-hand recipient's confident invitation to read in 69:19.
terra: The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, reversing the confident mouth that boasts of what it did with a mass of wealth.
terra: His cry هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَانِيَهْ turns the section's أَهْلَكْتُ boast into the loss of his own authority.
terra: The condemned wealth-boaster is seized and shackled, turning imagined personal power into bodily capture.
terra: He is inserted into a long chain, completing the restraint that stands opposite freeing another person's neck.

luna: The section explicitly sets feeding the hungry poor against the failure to encourage it; this ayah names that failure in the condemned person's conduct. | terra: His punishment is explained by his failure to urge feeding the needy, making the absent outward word part of the failure to nourish.

luna: The section cites feeding the poor and gives this as its contrary outcome: the condemned person has no food except ghislin. | terra: He has no food except foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the nourishing food he would not direct to a poor mouth.

luna: The section's cited 69:36 names ghislin as the only food; this next ayah adds that only the wrongdoers eat it, turning failed care for the poor into a boundary around who receives that food. | terra: Only the sinners eat that food, identifying the receiving mouths and completing the punitive meal of 69:36.
terra: The faithful recognize an assigned right in their wealth, making provision something already oriented beyond its possessor.
terra: That right belongs to the asker and the deprived, identifying both the requesting mouth and the need that another person's resources must answer.

luna: This ayah repeats أصحاب اليمين as a group label, echoing the section's derivation of الميمنة from the right-hand side. | terra: The people of the right are excepted from pledged captivity and question the guilty, preserving the right-side designation outside surah 90.
terra: Those in Saqar confess, “We did not feed the needy,” naming the failed inward use of food as a cause of judgment.
terra: They add that they joined those who plunged into vain discourse, placing corrupt outward talk beside the refusal to feed in 74:44.
terra: The human supposes God will not assemble his bones, making dismembered bodily parts the object of his doubt.
terra: God answers that He can proportion even the fingertips, an especially fine-grained craftsman image of reconstructing the body.
terra: At death the departing life reaches the collarbones, placing human helplessness at the very bodily region evoked by the section's terāʾib gloss.
terra: The human was a drop of emitted fluid, supplying the bodily material that God creates and proportions in 75:38.
terra: The drop becomes a clot and God creates and proportions it, another direct sequence of bodily material and measured making.
terra: From that made body God produces the male and female pair, completing the creation sequence of 75:37–38.

luna: The section moves from the body made to its use; this ayah describes a human made from a mixed drop and given hearing and sight for a test. | terra: Humanity is made from a mixed drop as a test and made hearing and seeing, joining bodily manufacture, endowed organs, and accountability in one claim.

luna: The section asks how the given faculties are used; this ayah pairs guidance to the way with the human's choice to be grateful or ungrateful. | terra: After the organs and test of 76:2, God guides the way and the human becomes grateful or ungrateful, matching the section's question of which direction the given tools take.

luna: The section's ط ع م discussion turns inward mouth-work toward the vulnerable; this ayah says the righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive. | terra: The righteous feed food they love to the needy, orphan, and captive, precisely realizing the turn from one's own appetite toward another mouth.

luna: The section asks what giving food is for; these feeders explain that they seek God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks. | terra: Their accompanying speech says they feed only for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, opposing the section's boastful utterance after spending.
terra: The human is created from a lowly fluid, recalling the material out of which the complete, upright body is made.
terra: The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, identifying the womb as the workshop-like enclosure of bodily formation.
terra: It remains there until a known measure, making bodily development a timed and fitted process.
terra: God says “We measured,” then praises the measurers, closing the scene on deliberate proportion rather than self-made power.
terra: The bodily act of frowning and turning away begins a rebuke over how one's face and attention are directed toward a vulnerable visitor.
terra: The visitor is identified by his blindness, making an impaired bodily faculty central to the ethical encounter.
terra: The self-sufficient person receives attention, reversing the section's demand that faculties and effort turn toward one in need.
terra: The one who comes striving is the person whose approach should receive attention, correcting the body's social direction in 80:1.
terra: The human is asked from what God created him, confronting pride by returning attention to bodily material.
terra: God creates him from a drop and proportions him, directly naming the fitting of the finished body.
terra: The human is commanded to look at his food, turning bodily sight toward reflection on what the mouth receives.
terra: The long account of rain, split earth, crops, and fruit culminates in provision for humans and their livestock, locating a meal within divine preparation.
terra: The human is asked what deceived him concerning his generous Lord, introducing 82:7–8's reminder that this Lord created, balanced, and assembled his body.

luna: The section's lexicographic reading of كَبَدٍ as upright and balanced creation is stated through Allah's creating, proportioning, and balancing the human. | terra: ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ names creation, proportioning, and balancing, the exact bodily senses developed from خلق and kebed.

luna: The section counts the body as crafted parts; رَكَّبَكَ describes Allah composing a person in whatever form He wills. | terra: God assembles the human in whatever form He wills, extending 82:7's image of a body deliberately fitted from parts.

luna: This judgment scene again gives the record to the right hand, making the bodily right-hand image a sign of an outcome, as in the section's right-side designation. | terra: Receiving one's book in the right hand marks the bodily side as the sign of a favorable reckoning.
luna: The section's right-side term derives from the hand; this paired scene gives the record from behind the back, an opposite bodily sign to the right hand.
luna: The section's bodily inventory includes the origin of a human body; this ayah asks what a person was created from and answers with a gushing fluid, setting up the next ayah.

luna: The section identifies its dictionary form ترائب as the necklace-place on the chest; this ayah places the issuing fluid between the backbone and ترائب. | terra: The reproductive fluid emerges from between backbone and تَرَائِب, the exact Qur'anic bodily sense of the root invoked through matraba.
terra: God “created and proportioned,” a concise parallel to the section's complete and balanced human construction.
terra: God measures and guides; following 87:2, this reproduces the section's sequence from fitted creation to directed use.
terra: The punished have no food except a bitter thorn, a meal that inverts the section's life-giving food offered in hunger.
terra: That food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, explicitly denying the two functions that make feeding another mouth merciful.
terra: “Your Lord is ever watchful” states the direct boundary on the section's belief that no one sees.

luna: The section's body-part inventory leads toward care for the orphan; this ayah challenges the claim to honor by pointing to failure to honor the orphan. | terra: The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” opens a sequence contrasting possessive wealth-use with care for the vulnerable.

luna: The section's ط ع م link is feeding a needy person; this ayah condemns failing to urge food for the poor. | terra: They do not urge one another to feed the needy, directly matching the mouth's failure to advocate food as well as to give it.

luna: The section turns a boast over wealth toward feeding others; this ayah names the contrary act of consuming inheritance indiscriminately. | terra: They consume inheritance in a devouring consumption, turning the eating mouth toward others' wealth rather than others' hunger.

luna: The section's speaker boasts about spending abundant wealth before the call to feed the needy; this ayah names an excessive love of wealth as part of the surrounding moral failure. | terra: Their excessive love of wealth explains the sequence's failure to honor and feed, illuminating the boast over amassed or expended المال.
terra: The oath turns to the self and the One who proportioned it, an inward counterpart to the section's upright, balanced bodily making.
terra: The fashioned self is inspired with both its wrong and its piety, a precise nonbodily parallel to endowed human capacity taking one of two directions.
terra: Giving and fearing God begin the path whose outcome is ease, directing possession outward rather than treating it as grounds for boast.
terra: The one who is miserly and regards himself as self-sufficient embodies the reverse direction of both feeding another and remembering one's made dependence.
terra: The most reverent person gives wealth to purify himself, a deliberate right use of property against the image of boastful expenditure.
terra: The orphan must not be oppressed, directing power toward the same vulnerable figure whom the section commands one to feed.
terra: The asker must not be repelled, governing the encounter between a needy person's requesting mouth and the addressee's response.
terra: God's favor is to be spoken of, making speech a grateful use of what was given rather than a boast of personal expenditure.

luna: The section gives chest as a lexicographic sense of بلد; this ayah's صَدْرِي is a directly bodily image of an opened chest. | terra: God's opening or expansion of the Prophet's chest gives direct Qur'anic bodily content to the section's secondary “balad as chest.”

luna: The section's alternative reading of كَبَدٍ as upright balance meets the same human-creation formula here: أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ makes the body's well-proportioned form explicit. | terra: The identical frame لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا ٱلْإِنسَانَ replaces the section's bodily kebed with “the best proportion,” directly confirming its upright, balanced reading.

luna: The next verse reverses the section's bodily uprightness and the preceding verse's best proportion by returning the human to the lowest state; the expression may mean bodily decline or another lower state, so the bodily reading is uncertain. | terra: After the best bodily proportion of 95:4, humanity is reduced to the lowest of the low, exposing the made form's vulnerability and moral limit.
terra: Faith and good deeds are excepted from 95:5's lowering after beautiful proportion, showing that bodily form reaches its proper outcome through action.
terra: The command to recite in the name of the creating Lord joins an outward act of the mouth to acknowledgment of the Maker.
terra: God creates the human from a clinging clot, grounding the reciting person of 96:1 in bodily dependence.
terra: The human transgresses, beginning the exact posture of self-assertion that culminates in the reminder that God sees in 96:14.
terra: His transgression arises because he sees himself as self-sufficient, closely paralleling the section's imagined immunity from another's power or sight.
terra: “Does he not know that God sees?” is the direct rhetorical answer to the section's self-assured man who supposes no one saw him.
terra: The passage begins with the slanderer and backbiter, a mouth turned toward injury before it turns to his relation with wealth.
terra: That same person gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, joining corrupt utterance to possessive accumulation.

luna: The section's speaker boasts of spending abundant wealth and imagines himself beyond anyone's power; this ayah depicts the opposite money-direction, hoarding and counting wealth, yet the same false confidence that wealth can secure lasting life. | terra: He supposes his wealth will make him immortal, exposing the same boastful delusion that bodily power and wealth escape their limit.

luna: The section calls for food on a day of hunger; this ayah says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear. | terra: God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, naming feeding as a divine gift that humans are then called to extend.

luna: The section directs the mouth and body toward an orphan in need; this ayah depicts the contrary bodily act of harshly repulsing the orphan. | terra: The denier physically repels the orphan, the social and bodily reverse of opening one's means toward the vulnerable.

luna: The section describes feeding the poor on a hungry day; this ayah condemns not urging others to feed the poor. | terra: He does not urge the feeding of the poor, a direct parallel to refusal of the steep path's إطعام.
